explanationCorrect: Self-hosted runners are selected by labels; listing multiple labels like [self-hosted, gpu] requires a runner that carries all of them, targeting your GPU machine.
explanationIncorrect: A single arbitrary string like gpu-runner-only only matches if a runner literally has that exact label, and it omits the self-hosted label that distinguishes your fleet from GitHub-hosted runners. uses: is for referencing actions, not selecting runners. There is no runner: label key; runner selection is expressed solely through runs-on labels.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Which mechanism lets an organization publish a starter workflow that repositories can adopt from the Actions tab?

options.text: A workflow-templates directory in the organization's .github repository
A required-workflows setting on each repo
A branch named starter in every repository
Enabling GitHub Pages for the organization

explanationCorrect: Placing workflow YAML plus a JSON properties file in the workflow-templates directory of the org's special .github repository surfaces those templates as starter workflows for member repositories.
explanationIncorrect: Required workflows enforce running a workflow but are a different feature from offering an adoptable starter template. A branch named starter has no special meaning to Actions and would not appear as a template. GitHub Pages publishes static websites and is entirely unrelated to distributing starter workflows.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: For security, why is it recommended not to run self-hosted runners on public repositories?

options.text: Forked pull requests could run untrusted code on your infrastructure
Public repositories cannot use self-hosted runners at all
Self-hosted runners cannot access the internet
GitHub bills extra minutes for public self-hosted runs

explanationCorrect: A malicious fork can open a pull request whose workflow executes arbitrary code; on a self-hosted runner that code runs on your own machine and network, which is why GitHub warns against it for public repos.
explanationIncorrect: It is technically possible to attach self-hosted runners to public repositories; the guidance is about risk, not an outright block. Self-hosted runners typically do have internet access, so that is not the concern. GitHub does not bill minutes for self-hosted runners at all since you provide the hardware, so extra billing is not the reason.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization admin wants secrets that many repositories share, managed centrally. What is the right feature?

options.text: Organization-level secrets with a repository access policy
Copying the same repository secret into each repo by hand
Committing the secret to a shared config file
Storing the secret as an environment variable in each workflow

explanationCorrect: Organization secrets are defined once and made available to selected or all repositories through an access policy, giving central management without duplication.
explanationIncorrect: Hand-copying a repository secret into every repo is exactly the duplication and drift that org secrets eliminate. Committing a secret to a file exposes it in the repository history and is a serious security mistake. Putting the value in a plain env variable in each workflow neither centralises it nor keeps it secret, since env values are visible in the workflow definition.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Which report helps an enterprise understand how many Actions minutes and storage are being consumed?

options.text: The billing and usage metrics for Actions in the organization or enterprise settings
The repository's Insights traffic graph
The Dependency graph
The Security overview

explanationCorrect: Actions minute and storage consumption is reported under the billing and usage sections of organization or enterprise settings, where you can also download usage reports.
explanationIncorrect: The Insights traffic graph tracks views and clones of a repository, not Actions consumption. The Dependency graph lists software dependencies for security and does not measure compute usage. The Security overview aggregates code and secret scanning alerts, which is unrelated to minutes and storage billing.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: You want to restrict the default permissions of GITHUB_TOKEN across all repositories in an organization to read-only by default. Where is this best set?

options.text: In the organization Actions settings, choosing the read-only default workflow permissions
By editing every workflow to add permissions: read-all
By rotating the token manually each day
By disabling the GITHUB_TOKEN feature

explanationCorrect: Organization Actions settings include a default workflow permissions choice; setting it to read-only applies that baseline to repositories, and workflows can still request more with an explicit permissions block.
explanationIncorrect: Editing every workflow is error-prone and does not enforce a baseline for new or unmodified workflows the way the org setting does. GITHUB_TOKEN is minted per run and does not need manual daily rotation, so that does not address default permissions. Disabling the token would break most workflows that need any repository access, which is far broader than tightening the default.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: What is the purpose of a runner group?

options.text: To control which organizations or repositories may use a set of self-hosted runners
To automatically scale GitHub-hosted runners
To group workflow jobs so they share a runner
To assign labels to GitHub-hosted runners

explanationCorrect: Runner groups are an access-control boundary for self-hosted runners, letting admins decide which repositories or organizations are allowed to send jobs to the runners in that group.
explanationIncorrect: Runner groups do not scale GitHub-hosted runners; those scale automatically and are not organised into your groups. They do not cause jobs to share a runner; each job still gets its own runner assignment. Labels apply to runners for targeting, but a runner group is about access scope, not label assignment on GitHub-hosted machines.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Which approach keeps sensitive cloud credentials out of long-lived secrets when workflows deploy to a cloud provider?

options.text: OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation to obtain short-lived credentials at run time
Storing the access keys as organization secrets
Printing the credentials to the log for auditing
Hard-coding the keys in the workflow file

explanationCorrect: OIDC lets a workflow exchange a signed identity token for short-lived cloud credentials via a trust policy, removing the need to store static long-lived keys as secrets.
explanationIncorrect: Storing static access keys as org secrets still keeps long-lived credentials around, which is exactly the risk OIDC removes. Printing credentials to logs exposes them even though the runner masks known secrets, and it is never an auditing practice. Hard-coding keys in the workflow file commits them to the repository, the worst option for secret handling.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An enterprise wants certain reusable workflows to run on every repository regardless of what the repo's own workflows contain. Which feature fits?

options.text: Required workflows configured at the organization level
A branch protection rule requiring status checks
A CODEOWNERS file listing the security team
A repository ruleset limiting who can push

explanationCorrect: Required (organization) workflows let admins enforce that a specified reusable workflow runs on pull requests across selected repositories, independent of the repositories' own workflow files.
explanationIncorrect: Branch protection status checks can require a check to pass but do not themselves inject or run a centrally defined workflow across many repositories. CODEOWNERS routes review requests and does not run any workflow. A ruleset limiting who can push governs write access, not the automatic execution of an enforced workflow.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Why might an organization mirror popular third-party actions into an internal repository and reference those copies?

options.text: To pin a reviewed version and reduce supply-chain risk from upstream changes
Because external actions cannot be used without mirroring
To make workflows run faster by avoiding the network
Because GitHub deletes third-party actions after 90 days

explanationCorrect: Mirroring lets a team vet a specific version of an action, control when it updates, and insulate their workflows from unexpected or malicious upstream changes, tightening the software supply chain.
explanationIncorrect: External actions can be used directly, so mirroring is a security choice rather than a requirement. Performance is not the motivation; the runner still checks out the action, and any speed difference is negligible compared with the supply-chain benefit. GitHub does not delete third-party actions after 90 days, so that is not a reason to mirror.
